### Option 1: Elevated Poetic Form
*This version preserves the original stanza structure, narrative detail, and satirical mock-heroic tone while elevating the diction, rhythm, and poetic resonance.*

**I. *Ille Ego***

O, harken to my call! For I aspire  
To catch the incandescent Chaucerian fire,  
And weave in solemn, doleful strains the tale  
Of Johnny Raw, across the distant vale—  
Who, driven by a desperate design  
To hold the public gaze in awe divine,  
Set off post-haste for distant Hindoostan,  
Astride Old Poulter’s mare to speed his plan.  

Tramp! tramp! across the continental strand,  
Splash! splash! he traversed ocean, sea, and land;  
And there gave vent to his boastful decree:  
“Pray tell, who rides with such mastery as me?  

“For I am he who boldly sallied forth  
To rout the classic masters of the North,  
And swore this steed possessed far greater worth  
Than Hector’s fiery chargers on the earth.  

“From his high throne grand Homer I deposed,  
And Virgil’s ancient majesty opposed;  
And in the stead of both, I dared elevate  
The doughty Mother Bunch to regal state.  

“To France I galloped on my trusty roan,  
Whose steadfast mettle never fear had known;  
There, perched atop the sacred tomb of Joan,  
I piped a dismal, melancholy tone.  

“A wild and wondrous stanza I intoned,  
To move my audience till they wept and moaned;  
Yet when I ceased and looked upon the deep,  
I found my listeners fast asleep!  

“Whereat a furious, solemn oath I swore,  
To seek a dire revenge forevermore;  
And summoned forth, to rouse their slumbering peak,  
The stalwart Taffy bearing high his leek.  

“To Heaven and Hell I boldly rode away,  
Undaunted by the storm or tempest’s sway;  
Concocted there a dark, infernal lay,  
And cast a curse upon them in dismay.  

“Now rise, O Proteus, changeful seer of old,  
To embolden this my steed with spirit bold;  
Assume all wild transfigurations there,  
Save those which Taste and noble Nature wear!”

***

Hear my account, for I intend to channel the poetic spirit of Chaucer and deliver, in somber and lamenting verse, the tale of Johnny Raw. Driven by an audacious desire to command public astonishment, he embarked at full speed for Hindoostan, mounted upon Old Poulter’s mare. 

Traversing land and sea with relentless momentum, he ultimately unleashed his boastful pride, declaring: *“Who among men can ride as I do? For I am the hero who rode forth to vanquish the classical masters, declaring this mare superior to both of Hector’s legendary warhorses. I dethroned Homer, struck down Virgil, and exalted the humble Mother Bunch in their stead.*

*“Astride my roan—whose steadfast courage no force could intimidate—I galloped to France, perched upon the tomb of Joan of Arc, and played a mournful song. I sang a wild, extraordinary composition intended to bring my audience to tears; yet when I concluded and observed the crowd, I found them sound asleep.*

*“In response, I swore a vengeful oath to exact retribution and summoned the stout figure of Taffy with his leek to provoke a reaction. I then rode undeterred through wind and foul weather to Heaven and Hell, where I devised an infernal song and cursed the entire assembly.*

*“Now, I invoke Proteus, the shapeshifting prophet, to inspire my mare—granting her any form imaginable, save for those governed by genuine Taste and Nature.”*

### The Unholy Odyssey of Johnny Raw

The speaker begins by recounting the fantastical and foolish tale of Johnny Raw, an ambitious soul driven by a desperate craving for public renown. In a bid to capture the world's imagination, Johnny embarks on an arduous, ill-conceived pilgrimage toward the distant shores of Hindoostan. His chosen transport for this grand spectacle is neither a gilded chariot nor a mighty stallion, but a humble, unlikely mare, upon which he pins all his hopes for everlasting fame.

As he travels, Johnny’s vanity quickly outpaces his modesty. He brags endlessly to anyone who will listen, declaring that his unassuming mare is far superior to the legendary war horses of history and myth. His arrogance, however, is not limited to horsemanship; it extends deeply into the realm of literature. With delusional grandeur, Johnny proclaims himself the supreme master of verse, boasting that his own poetic talents have utterly overthrown the classical giants of antiquity, leaving Homer and Virgil vanquished in his creative wake.

Seeking an audience worthy of his self-proclaimed genius, Johnny makes a grand stop in France to showcase his art. Taking the stage, he delivers what he believes to be a deeply moving, wild, and passionate song, fully expecting his listeners to be overcome with emotion and brought to tears. Reality, however, delivers a humiliating blow. Rather than weeping at his brilliance, the French audience finds his performance so excruciatingly dull that they are promptly lulled into a deep, unanimous sleep. 

Enraged by the crowd's apathy, Johnny’s hurt pride curdles into a monstrous desire for vengeance. Refusing to accept his own mediocrity, he resolves to punish humanity for its failure to appreciate him. He embarks on a dark, metaphysical pilgrimage, traversing the realms of both Heaven and Hell. Drawing upon the celestial and the infernal, he crafts a diabolical, cursed song designed not to entertain, but to torment and hex all who hear it.

In a dramatic climax to his madness, Johnny turns to ancient magic to solidify his revenge. He invokes Proteus, the shapeshifting god of the sea, pleading with the deity to bestow his mare with unnerving, fluid transformations. Johnny does not seek beauty or grace, but horror; he demands that his steed assume grotesque and monstrous forms specifically designed to offend good taste, defy the laws of nature, and serve as an everlasting monument to his bitter, spiteful defiance.

In the grand annals of literature, few names were spoken with as much self-inflicted reverence as that of Johnny Raw. A man of limitless vanity and painfully limited talent, Johnny possessed a singular, burning ambition: to dethrone the classical literary giants of old. Homer was a dotard, Shakespeare a mere scribbler of trite melodramas, and Milton terribly unimaginative. Johnny was convinced that the world did not need harmony, truth, or human nature in its poetry—it needed shock, gloom, and pure, unfiltered sensationalism. He would force humanity, and whatever lay beyond it, to bow before the terrifying majesty of his genius.

With a leather-bound portfolio under his arm and a chest swollen with self-importance, Johnny set out on a grand pilgrimage across the globe. From the fog-choked alleyways of London to the sun-bleached ruins of Greece, he sought audiences to enlighten. Standing atop tables in crowded taverns and mounting the steps of royal academies, he unveiled his masterpiece of "unnatural verse." 

His poetry was a tempest of dismal absurdities. He spurned simple, beautiful imagery in favor of violent, unnatural juxtapositions. He bellowed stanzas about *"The Bleeding Sockets of the Lunar Void"* and *"The Spleen-Drenched Miasma of the Unborn Worm."* Johnny expected his listeners to weep, to tremble, or to go mad from the sheer, apocalyptic weight of his vision. 

Yet, mortal audiences proved strangely resistant to his genius. Finding the earth’s critics too pedestrian, Johnny sought higher—and lower—realms. Driven by his unyielding conceit, he traversed supernatural thresholds, marching boldly into the shimmering courts of the Fae, the ethereal halls of Olympus, and even the shadowed depths of the Underworld. Surely, he reasoned, the dark specters and immortal beings of the abyss would recognize a kindred, tortured soul.

In a grand, subterranean amphitheater where demons, ghosts, and ancient deities had gathered, Johnny Raw took the stage. The air was thick with sulfur and dread. The immortal audience looked on with cold, terrifying gazes, expecting a mortal soul to shatter in their presence. 

Instead, Johnny cleared his throat, struck a dramatic pose, and began to read his grandest epic—a ten-thousand-line atrocious cacophony designed to shock the cosmos into submission.

*"O, Screaming Void of Bile and Bone!"* Johnny roared, his voice echoing off the obsidian walls. *"Tear loose the Sinews of the Sun! Let Chaos drown in Shadow’s Groan, where Nothingness is twice undone!"*

He gestured wildly to the heavens. He stomped his feet. He shrieked verses of dismal gloom, unnatural horrors, and forced, discordant rhymes. On and on he went, painting pictures of exaggerated decay and contrived madness, waiting for the supernatural legion to recoil in awe.

Minute turned into hour. Page turned into page. 

Slowly, the atmosphere in the cavernous realm began to shift. The fiery glare of the demons dimmed. A high demon of the pit, bent on eternal torment, rested his heavy, horned head on his clawed fist. Beside him, a phantom queen let her ghostly eyelids flutter shut. The ancient specters, who had endured millennia of agony, found themselves overwhelmed by a new, far more potent force: utter, soul-crushing boredom.

Johnny’s verses were so endlessly dismal, so void of rhythm, heart, or natural truth, that their shocking imagery collapsed under the weight of its own monotony. The "unnatural" had simply become tedious. 

By line three thousand, a soft rumble competed with Johnny's thunderous recitation. It was not the roaring approval of the damned, nor the terror of gods—it was a chorus of rhythmic, heavy snoring. 

When Johnny finally reached his triumphant, earth-shattering climax, striking a final, triumphant posture with arms outstretched, he opened his eyes to behold his audience. The mighty beings of the supernatural cosmos were slumped over one another, fast asleep. A dread lord of chaos was softly drooling onto his velvet robes. 

Johnny stood alone in the quiet, punctuated only by the puffing breath of sleeping specters. His grand crusade had ended not in terror, nor in praise, but in a profound, somnambulistic stupor.

In his quest to eclipse the masters, Johnny Raw had proved a timeless truth: art cannot live on sensation alone. In banishing nature, emotion, and beauty from his verse in exchange for cheap, dismal shock value, he had created nothing more than a glorified lullaby. His pretentious efforts had failed entirely, leaving his name not carved in the pantheon of literary gods, but forgotten in the quiet, heavy sleep of a thoroughly bored universe.
outputs.L5:
**The Poet in the Mirror: *Ego*, *Ille*, and the Chaucerian Persona**

In the opening lines attributed to Virgil’s *Aeneid*—*Ille ego, qui quondam gracili modulatus avena* (“I am that man who once tuned his song on a slender reed”)—classical antiquity established a profound poetic gesture: the synthesis of the self (*Ego*) and the external, historicized identity (*Ille*). To say *Ego* is to claim subjective, immediate experience; to say *Ille* is to step back, viewing oneself or the world as an objective "other." Centuries later, at the dawn of English literature, Geoffrey Chaucer mastered this delicate interplay, transforming the tension between *Ego* and *Ille* into the defining hallmark of his narrative art.

Chaucer lived in a fourteenth-century world caught between medieval scholasticism and the early sparks of Renaissance humanism. In his masterpiece, *The Canterbury Tales*, this philosophical duality finds its literary form through the creation of the narrator persona—often called "Chaucer the Pilgrim." Here, Chaucer splits his authorial identity. The *Ego* is the wide-eyed, slightly naive narrator who moves among the travelers at the Tabard Inn, claiming merely to record what he sees and hears without judgment. This *Ego* presents himself as a foolish, well-meaning chronicler, famously claiming to have little wit.

Yet, behind this humble *Ego* operates the master craftsman—the silent, observing *Ille*. *Ille* is the detached genius, the author standing outside the frame, guiding the satire with supreme ironic skill. When the narrator (*Ego*) lavishly praises the corrupt Friar or the hypocritical Prioress, the reader hears the quiet laughter of the poet (*Ille*) echoing behind the words. Chaucer uses *Ego* as a mask, allowing him to infiltrate the diverse tapestry of medieval society without imposing immediate moral condemnation.

Furthermore, this dynamic extends beyond the narrator to the pilgrims themselves. In Chaucer’s art, every character exists in a state of friction between their projected *Ego* (how they wish to be seen) and the *Ille* (who they truly are, revealed through their tales and unconscious slips). The Wife of Bath, in her magnificent prologue, fiercely asserts her subjective *Ego*—her desires, her autonomy, her lived experience—against the distant, authoritative *Ille* of male medieval doctrine. The Pardoner, conversely, suffers a tragic fracture of the self: he openly confesses his greed (his true *Ego*), yet relies on the performative illusion of sanctity (*Ille*) to manipulate his audience.

By bridging *Ego* and *Ille*, Chaucer did something revolutionary for English letters. He moved away from the monolithic, anonymous voice of early medieval allegory and introduced a deeply psychological, polyphonic realism. He recognized that human beings are simultaneously the subject of their own stories (*Ego*) and the objects of a broader, often absurd world (*Ille*). 

When we read Chaucer today, we are invited into this very dialectic. We see ourselves in his flawed, vibrant characters; we recognize our own private *Ego* in the universal *Ille* of human nature. Like the ancient Latin poets before him, Chaucer looked into the mirror of his art and created a space where the individual "I" and the eternal "Other" could finally speak in the same tongue.

counterfactuals.output:
Sing, O ye Muses, loud and shrill,
Of triumphs fought and won,
Not on the plains of ancient Troy,
But down at *The Grind & Scone*!
Sing of the knight of velvet scarf,
The prince of pretentious prose,
Sir Johnny Raw, whose mega-ego
Reached where no laurel grows.

With thrift-store tweed and beret cocked,
And notebook bound in leather,
He nursed an oat-milk cardamoin,
Ignoring rainy weather.
"The Ancients," sneered the youthful bard,
"Are dusty, dead, and dry!
Old Homer was a total hack,
And Virgil lied—but *I*—

"I speak the raw, unvarnished truth!
I feel the world’s deep ache!"
He tapped his Bic against his chin,
And swore the earth would shake.
He summoned up the tragic shade
Of Homer, blind and old,
Who walked the stage in sandals worn,
To sing of spears and gold.

Great Homer struck a bronze-strung lyre,
And sang Achilles' rage,
Of wine-dark seas and crashing shields
That echoed down the age.
But Johnny raised a pale, limp hand:
"Enough of bronze and gore!
Your dactyls drag! Your tropes are toxic!
Homer, you’re a bore!

"What care we for the siege of Troy?
Have you experienced *me*?
Behold my nine-page unrhymed piece
On bad astrology!"
He read a line with tortured sighs,
And gestured toward the ceiling:
*“the moon is a blue bruised turnip /
of my disassociated feeling.”*

Poor Homer gasped; his lyre broke;
He clutched his silver beard.
Before such raw, unstructured dreck,
The ancient poet feared!
He fled into the Underworld,
Defeated, crushed, and small,
While Johnny Raw smirked at the room
And leaned against the wall.

Then rose the ghost of Virgil next,
In Roman mantle grand,
And spat a line of Latin grace
Across the modern land:
*“Arma virumque cano—”* he began,
With majesty and art,
Executing perfect hexameter
To pierce the human heart.

“Hold on!” cried Johnny, waving high
A latte-stained critique,
“Your imperialist propaganda
Is utterly antique!
You wrote for Caesar! You're a sellout!
A shill for Rome’s domain!
Behold my lower-case masterwork
On mild emotional pain!”

Then Johnny cleared his youthful throat,
And whispered to the mic:
*“i am a leaf / bruised by a car /
on a street I do not like.”*

The Mantuan bard fell to his knees,
His scroll dropped to the floor!
“Alas!” wept Virgil, “Elegance
Can conquer man no more!
Such shallow nonsense, so profound
In its complete conceit!
I yield the crown to Johnny Raw,
My ruin is complete!”

The ghosts vanished in the neon glow,
The battle had been won!
The boldest poet of the age
Had eclipsed the ancient sun!
Sir Johnny smiled a victor’s smile,
And waited for the cheer,
To hear the thunderous applause
Of critics far and near.

He looked around the coffee shop
To claim his grand crusade—
And met the bored barista’s eyes,
Who wiped the espresso blade.
No crowd was there, no laurels green,
No swooning, breathless throngs—
Just one grey dachshund sound asleep,
Unmoved by modern songs.

Yet Johnny adjusted his beret,
And tweeted to the skies:
*“Destroyed two dead white guys tonight.
Art will again arise.”*

**THE KEHAMA-IAD; OR, THE LAUREATE’S SLUMBER**
*A Mock-Epic Fragment in the Sublime Style of Mr. S—th—y*

**CANTO I.**

I.
Arise, O Proteus, from the briny main!
In shapes grotesque assist my ponderous strain!
Shift as thou wilt—from monster into mud—
To match the heavy current of my blood;
For I, high Bard of dismal, dread renown,
Prepare to lay a blight upon the town,
And weave a song of such tremendous weight
As palls the Muse and paralyzes State!

II.
Away, fond Fancy! To the Orient far!
I mount my steed to seek the Eastern star!
No fiery Pegasus my thigh bestrides,
No winged griffin through the ether glides;
On *Old Poulter’s mare* I take my solemn way—
A wall-eyed nag of wretched, bone-bare grey!
Through dust and mire to *Hindoostan* we trot,
To sing of magic realms the world forgot.

III.
With dismal tales of necromancers grim,
And endless chants, and idols pale and dim,
I string ten thousand lines of heavy verse—
Each book a burden, and each page a curse!
A tale so dark, so tedious, and so deep,
It lulls the fiery soul of youth to sleep;
The reader yawns; the critic drops his head,
And lords and ladies slumber as if dead.

IV.
Plod on, good mare! Though all the nation snore,
We’ll ride and rhyme till time shall be no more!
Let Byron scoff, let lesser wits blaspheme,
My grandest triumph is the general dream:
While Orient spires in gloomy fog expire,
I damp the nation’s sense, and douse the Muse’s fire!

Put down your Homer, burn your scrolls, throw Virgil in the sea!
For history has finally birthed a poet supreme: **ME!**
Achilles was a whiny brat, Odysseus took too long,
And Gilgamesh was amateur compared to my main song!

*Tramp! tramp! across the land...*
*Splash! splash! across the sea!*
No epic poet was half so grand,
Or half as brilliant as me!

Old Beowulf fought one swamp hag, then called himself a king,
While I face dangers deadlier every time I try to sing!
The *Aeneid* was a bore-fest meant to flatter Roman snobs,
While my artistic genius moves the masses into sobs!

*Tramp! tramp! across the land...*
*Splash! splash! across the sea!*
They bow and grovel where I stand,
To hear my poetry!

I took the stage in Athens town and launched into Canto One,
I sang for seven straight-up days beneath the blazing sun!
The audience was paralyzed—their eyes began to glaze!
A dozen fell into a swoon, unconscious from my praise!

*Tramp! tramp! across the land...*
*Splash! splash! across the sea!*
My gift is more than they can stand,
This wondrous melody!

"Please, mercy, stop!" a fellow screamed, enraptured by my verse,
"He’s killing us!" a woman sobbed, as though under a curse.
They threw old turnips at my feet—a gift of local lore!
And half the tavern bolted out to tell the world some more!

*Tramp! tramp! across the land...*
*Splash! splash! across the sea!*
They squirm and snore at my command,
In solemn majesty!

I see them sleeping in their chairs, stunned silent by my art,
A crowd so overcome by beauty, tearing them apart!
They lay their heads upon the wood and weep until they sleep,
For passion such as mine, my friends, is infinitely deep!

So let the ancient legends fade, their dusty tropes can die,
No mortal man has ever scaled a peak as high as I!
And though the hall is empty now, and patrons fled in fear,
I know they’ll dream of me tonight, with glory in their ear!

*Tramp! tramp! across the land...*
*Splash! splash! across the sea!*
The greatest gift to all mankind
Is clearly, truly **ME!**

Gadzooks and huzzah for Sir Percival Pry,
The greatest of bards ’neath the glorious sky!
With a feather-capped hat and his ego swelling,
And a talent for remarkably terrible spelling.

Upon a grey nag that was bony and slow
(Which he dubbed "Bucephalus," mighty and low),
He packed up his parchment, his ink, and his pride,
And announced to the village: "To India I ride!"

"For England is small for a genius like me!
My prose must expand to the shores of the sea!
The Rajahs and Tigers are desperate to hear
My twelve-hundred-page heroic epic, *My Dear*!"

So off trotted Percy, a quill in his hand,
Composing grand odes as he rode through the land.
With a bump and a jolt, every letter was blurred,
Yet he swore ’twas the finest the world ever heard.

He scribbled through France while asleep in the seat,
He rhymed in the Alps, though the horse lost its feet.
"Step backward, Lord Byron! Move over, Will Shakespeare!
My stanza on radishes brings men to tears!"

Through deserts he trotted, ink splashed on his nose,
Enlightening camels with wretched high prose.
He shouted to sandstorms, "Behold my refrain!
No scribe in creation has so vast a brain!"

The nag gave a groan as they crossed the frontier,
Her rider still raving of "dactyls" and "cheer."
And after three years of a tail-breaking pace,
They reached the grand heat of a tropical place.

He rode into town with his chin in the air,
Unrolling a scroll as the villagers stared.
"Rejoice, O Great India!" Sir Percival cried,
"The Emperor of Literature finally has arrived!"

The horse gave a sigh and collapsed in the dirt,
As Percy read verse forty-two to his shirt.
And though not a soul understood what he said,
He declared himself King, put his quill to his head,
And wrote a new poem: *How I Conquered the East*—
While eating a curry, still sitting on his beast.
